utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. I see, Mr. Hannis, that the Prosecution team is not exactly the same as it was yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. With me to my immediate left is Mr. Stephen Margetts, who has been here before with Mr. Harmon, and he will be leading our first witness this morning, Mr. Hasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. And on the Defence side, I see that Mr. Stewart is still busy elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. We anticipate that he will probably be returning tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then there is another issue. I am informed that the parties were meeting yesterday and they would like to continue their meeting today. I'm not going to ask you exactly what progress you make, but of course it's the understanding of the Chamber that if we would limit ourselves to just hearing the testimony of one witness today, that both parties are convinced that it's worth the investment of not hearing any other evidence today, but rather, to spend the time on the continuation of their communication. I see that this is confirmed by nodding, so therefore, the Chamber agrees with the proposal that we would have a court hearing of limited time today. I do understand that it's one witness. Yes. I now have the list in front of me. It's Mr. Hasanovic. There will be no -- there are no protective measures effective. Mr. Usher, would you then, please, escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Margetts, awaiting the arrival of the witness: The statement of Mr. Hasanovic has not been filed yet, since it's an 89(F) witness; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if it's clear that a witness will appear as an 89(F) witness, I think the Chamber would like to have an opportunity to then read, if that's clear, to read his statement in advance. So now, at least, if the first thing you do is to tender his statement, so that we can more easily follow --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, before giving evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this declaration is handed out to you now by the usher, and I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hasanovic. Please be seated. You'll first be addressed by counsel for the Prosecution, Mr. Margetts. Mr. Margetts, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Resid Hasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In April 2000, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY in respect to events that took place in Bratunac in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, pursuant to Rule 89(F), may the Office of the Prosecutor's statement be given the next exhibit number and shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, that would be --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P72.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If the witness could be handed a B/C/S version and the English version could be provided to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, do you recall giving this statement to the ICTY investigators on the 7th of April, 2000?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And since you've arrived in The Hague recently, have you been given an opportunity to review the statement?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Are the matters set out in the statement true and correct?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I proceed with an oral summary of the evidence set out in the statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic was the president of the SDA in the local community of Suha in the Bratunac municipality before the war. In his statement, Mr. Hasanovic describes the political and military situation in Bratunac prior to the war, including the military build-up in areas surrounding Bratunac, political tensions between the SDS and the SDA, the killing of two Muslim men in Kravica, and an attempt made by the JNA to seize military records. In April 1992, the police in Bratunac were divided and the Muslims and non-Serbs agreed to hand over their weapons. Mr. Hasanovic received information that the leader of the Serb Crisis Staff, Miroslav Deronjic, went to Pale on around the 13th of April, 1992 to meet with Radovan Karadzic to discuss and organise the takeover of Bratunac. On 17 April 1992, paramilitary groups, including Arkan's and Seselj's men, arrived in Bratunac. After the paramilitary groups arrived, regular soldiers from the Novi Sad and Uzice Corps also arrived. The Serbs took control of the town. Muslim men were taken away from their homes and killed. Houses were broken into and deserted property was claimed by the newly formed Serb state. The Serbs specified a 29 April 1992 deadline for the non-Serb population to sign documents pledging loyalty to the new Serbian territory of Birac. Between the 10th and 29th of April, many of the non-Serb population left the area. A unit of the JNA came to the village of Suha, where Mr. Hasanovic lived, and they set a deadline for the hand-over of weapons. Subsequently, Mr. Hasanovic's home was searched for weapons by JNA officers. On the 1st of May, 1992, Srebrenica was attacked. That was the adjoining municipality to Bratunac, to the south. On 9 May 1992, Mr. Hasanovic observed military and paramilitary soldiers all over Bratunac and was warned that he could be killed travelling in Bratunac. On or about the 10th of May, 1992, Mr. Hasanovic's village of Suha was attacked. He fled to the woods and the Serbs announced by megaphone that if the men did not surrender, their wives and children would be killed. Mr. Hasanovic surrendered and was taken toward the stadium in Bratunac and then on toward the Vuk Karadzic school. Whilst detained in the Vuk Karadzic school, he witnessed beatings and he saw dead bodies. He himself was beaten severely and slashed with a knife on the head and the arm. Mr. Hasanovic was then taken to the Bratunac stadium and gathered with about 5.000 people who had also been expelled from their homes. The women were forced to turn over their valuables and then they and the children were placed on buses and transferred out of the municipality. The men were separated from the women, and at this time Mr. Hasanovic saw a man being beaten and stabbed. Mr. Hasanovic, together with about 500 other men, returned to the Vuk Karadzic school, where he remained for two days in inhumane conditions. He observed many beatings and killings. Little, if any, food was provided to these men, and people that were brought in during the course of the men's detainment reported that homes were being destroyed in Bratunac and people were being burned alive in their homes. On or around the 13th of May, 1992, Mr. Hasanovic and other prisoners were transported to Pale, where they were detained in a sports hall. There were isolated beatings and they received very little food. On or around the 16th of May, Mr. Hasanovic, together with the other men detained in the sports hall in Pale, was exchanged. As a result of his maltreatment, apart from the wounds received referred to earlier, he suffered a ruptured kidney and, after the exchange, he remained hospitalised for 28 days. The evidence that Mr. Hasanovic will provide is primarily relevant to paragraphs 19, 24, and 27 of the indictment in this proceeding, and each of the counts 1 to 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I now proceed with the questioning of the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Just one small comment. Obviously, I have the statement, but it would be useful if I had been provided with the summary prior to coming in to court this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that would be a good idea, if it's prepared anyhow, then that -- Madam Registrar, could I just ask you whether it would be possible to make a printout of the part of the transcript which contains the summary, so that Ms. Loukas has a copy. Ms. Loukas, the registrar will now produce a copy of the part of the transcript which contains the summary of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed. Or do you have a copy with you, Mr. Margetts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's helpful, in the most part, with some small alteration, the summary that I have just read into the record is in fact the 65 ter summary. The amended 65 ter was served on the Defence on the 9th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, if you could print out that part of the transcript, then we have a literal --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I would just indicate, Your Honour, that this is a witness who I was provided for -- with additional proofing notes, and in those circumstances, I would have appreciated a copy of the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least you'll have it in a couple of minutes. Well, we can't do anything else at this very moment. Mr. Margetts, please proceed in your examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, you are from the Suha area in Bratunac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to show the witness a map which is listed as the second document on the exhibit list. May this map be given an exhibit number and presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P73.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, could you look at the map which is on the projector next to you. Was this map presented to you at the offices of the Prosecutor on the 18th of April, 2004?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Have you pre-marked this map and signed it?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, could you point to the marking which is marked number 1.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What does this cross designate?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: That marking approximately denotes the place where my house used to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Could you point to the marking which is marked number 2.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What does that mark designate?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: It designates the Vuk Karadzic school, where we were held captive for three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Is the cross marked on a particular building?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's precisely on the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Is that the building where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Could you point to the mark number 3.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What does that mark designate?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: It designates the stadium where civilians from Bratunac, Suha, and other areas, were held, most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, we'll discuss the Vuk Karadzic school and the stadium later in your evidence, but I'd now like to turn to a couple of other matters. At paragraph 37 of your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, you referred to a deadline being set for Muslims to sign loyalty oaths. How were the Muslims informed that they were to report and sign those loyalty oaths?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: It was mostly on an individual basis. People would be invited and then sent to populated areas to tell people to go to Serbian municipal buildings, town halls, to sign a document against which their property and all their other rights would be guaranteed. But if these people failed to appear, then there would be no guarantees. In my case, a neighbour came to see me, a neighbour who worked for the electrical company, and this neighbour informed me that I had to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When you arrived at the municipal hall, what did you observe?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I arrived with a group of my neighbours. I was very scared and anxious when I came there to the town hall. In that room, there was a desk and two people behind that desk, or perhaps more of them. They gave us these papers to sign, and of course we did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What did the loyalty oath say?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you the exact wording, but the main thing that I remember was that it said we were loyal citizens of the Bratunac municipalities, that we are signing this document, and in exchange for that signature, they are going to guarantee the safety of our property and our freedom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: After you signed this loyalty oath, was there a subsequent gathering in your village of Suha?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the signing of the loyalty oath, perhaps a day or two later, we received new information over megaphones driven around by military vehicles, and an announcement was made inviting all men to assemble at a certain point in town. And of course, we had to comply. We came to that place, which was close to the town church, and there we were addressed by a military officer. I think he had the rank of captain. He had come accompanied by a couple of soldiers. He held a short speech in front of us, saying that they knew that we had weapons. We had to hand over these weapons. It was up to us, but it would be better for us to surrender the weapons, because only in that case would they be able to guarantee our freedom and safety. They said somebody would come to pick up the weapons. And that meeting was over at that. We went back home and then things continued on that course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Was the captain accompanied by other soldiers; and if so, how many?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a number of soldiers in those two vehicles. Four or five soldiers, perhaps. And in addition to that, there were other soldiers in Bratunac who had come, either on foot or on various vehicles. In any case, there were people milling around during the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Was a deadline given to you to hand in the weapons?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were given a deadline. I believe that deadline was the very next day, or maybe even the day when we had been assembled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, 1992, you took your daughter to a clinic in Bratunac. On your return trip back home from the clinic, what did you observe?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I observed a very difficult situation, an abnormal situation. A lot of soldiers, commotion in the streets, and there was something heavy hanging in the air. People were scared. You could see nobody but soldiers on the streets. They were all wearing military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: On the 10th of May, 1992, at what time did you wake up?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of May -- that is, on the 9th of May, I had a very difficult night. There was a lot of shooting in the direction of Srebrenica from heavy arms, mostly from the direction of Bratunac. We were all scared. I was very worried. Just before the dawn, I managed to get some sleep; however, around 8.00 or 9.00 in the morning, I was woken up by heavy shooting from rifles. It looked as if it was happening right in front of my window. I jumped to my feet, and I saw that it was happening a bit further. I went out of the house. On the left-hand side, the village of Mihaljevici, above the Drina on the border with Serbia, had already been ablaze.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: It was very difficult to decide what to do. I said to my wife that I had to lie low. I saw fire and shots from surrounding mountains. I didn't know where to go. I went and hid in some bushes, in some nearby bushes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: From where you were positioned in these bushes, what could you see?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I could see my house, the road leading to the centre of the town, and after a while, if you will allow me to continue, I saw a column of women, children, and elderly people, and I could see people approaching the nearby houses and driving people from those houses and directing them towards the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did you hear any announcements being made?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was an announcement to the people, ordering them not to lock their houses, to go to Bratunac. And it was also said that the soldiers who were driving people out of the houses wanted to protect us. People then wondered who the protection was supposed to be from. And the answer was that some people came to Bratunac, Arkan's people, Seselj's people, and they wanted to protect us. And the only place where we could be protected was if we were all gathered in the stadium. And for a while we believed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When you were hiding, was there an announcement made directed to the men who were hiding?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: There was terror. Children were crying. Women were crying. There were elderly people who were shouting because they were told that if the people who went into hiding didn't come out of the hiding, that their families would not be guaranteed safety, that these people would be killed. People, elderly people, parents, would go and search the bushes to find their sons. We decided then to stop hiding because we thought that we should be with our families.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And did you surrender and join your family?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I joined my family. I found my wife and my children, and together with them, I started walking towards the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Can you describe the soldiers that were walking with the people?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: The soldiers mostly wore the uniforms of the Yugoslav army. They were mostly our neighbours from Bratunac, some of whom we recognised. I recognised two soldiers who were walking near me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Can you name those men?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One of them was Bozo Petkovic, and the other was Novak Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In which direction did you walk?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: We walked on the road leading to the centre of town, on the road leading towards the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: As you were walking, did you recognise any Serbs in military uniform who you knew?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as we came to the main road, in front of a shop whose owner was a Bosniak, I saw a group of young men sitting, wearing all sorts of military uniforms or paramilitary uniforms. A colleague of mine recognised me. He worked in the mine. I was his foreman. He approached me. He wore a black uniform that belonged to the mine. He wore black leather gloves, and he had two pistols. I was terrified. And then he told me: There you go. The time has come for me to decide what you are going to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What was his name, and did he have any insignia on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. His name was Novak Stjepanovic, also known as Krke, and he wore Arkan's insignia, and he also had a very, very long beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When you approached the stadium, did you see Stjepanovic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: As we were already close to this stadium, to my left, a car approached. I recognised the car. Two soldiers came out of the car. One of them was Krke. He stopped by the car. The soldiers approached me, asked me to identify myself. They told me that I had to go to the SUP, where I would give a statement. I was scared. My wife was scared. I tried to put up some resistance; however, they grabbed me by the arms and they took me on the road leading towards the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What did your son do?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: My son was 9 at the time. He was pulling me back. He started crying: Please don't take my dad away. They disregarded his cries. They just pushed him away and threw him on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You said you recognised the car that Stjepanovic was in. Who did that car belong to?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: The car belonged to another neighbour of mine who worked at the petrol station. His name was Safet Karin [as interpreted]. And the vehicle was a Kadett, a German car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Later that day, did you see Safet Karin?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I entered the school building, at the very entrance, I recognised the dead body of Safet Karic, who was laying on his stomach in the toilet of the school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt for one second. Your testimony, you told us about a person Safet Karin, and then, two lines later, it is Safet Karic. Is that the same person? And could you tell us what exactly his name is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that you are mistaken here. I referred -- I talked about Novak Stjepanovic as Krke, and the other person is Safet Karic, a Bosniak, who was killed in Bratunac, a person who worked at the petrol station. His name was Safet Karic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I listened carefully to you, and I looked at the transcript, and the first two times when you mentioned the name of Safet Karic, it sounded like Karin. It has been transcribed as Karin. So you say the person to whom the car belonged is named Safet Karic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, for the purposes of addressing the fate of Safet Karic, I have moved forward. I'll now take you back to your meeting with Stjepanovic. After you met Stjepanovic and you were taken away from your family, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I was taken to the Vuk Karadzic school, to a room next to the sports hall. They gave me a piece of paper and a pencil. They told me what the charges against me were, and those were that I was supposed to have killed some Serbs. I was the one who distributed arms amongst members of my party. They knew that, and I was supposed to write it down. I knew that this was all a lie. I refused to write it down. They were enraged and they told me: Very well, then. If you don't want to write it down, then you'll start singing as soon as you see how we kill your people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Can I take you back to when you arrived at the school. Can you describe the soldiers that were with Stjepanovic and took you to the school.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: They were mostly soldiers wearing military uniforms, with weapons, and I recognised most of them as citizens of Bratunac. There were some people I didn't recognise, and I'm sure that they belonged to the corps that came from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Vuk Karadzic school, how many soldiers did you observe, and did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: There were a lot of soldiers. According to my estimate, there were about 30 soldiers around the school that they were guarding. I recognised one soldier. His name was Dusan. He was also a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name of Bube Ristanovic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Bube Ristanovic, I recognised him at the entrance to the school. He was one of the guards. He held an automatic rifle. And during my three-day stay at the school, I would see him very often at the door, and sometimes he would also enter the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Was he a local man?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Bube Ristanovic was a citizen of Bratunac. Actually, he lived in Seliste hamlet. He was one of the athletes of the Guber sports team from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You have previously described the fate of Safet Karic. Can you tell me what you saw when you entered the Vuk Karadzic school.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: When I entered the Vuk Karadzic school, I saw to my left in the sports hall people who were lined by the wall. Some held three fingers in the air. Some were on the ground. Some were being beaten with wooden bats and metal rods. On the right-hand side, there were some other people sitting on benches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Immediately when you entered the school, did you see any bodies?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... it isn't appropriate to lead on something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it because I couldn't hear the first part of your objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it really isn't appropriate to lead on something like "Did you see any bodies?" I mean, the fact is the statement is before Your Honours, it's been admitted. The witness in fact has the statement in front of him. If the Prosecution are going to ask questions like "Did you see any bodies?" which do suggest the answer, it's a little silly, Your Honour, procedurally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, of course, if the statement is in front of the witness, then if this is an accepted procedure, then leading has a different meaning from --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, but one wonders what the point is when the Bench has the statement, the witness has the statement in front of them. If there's something sought to be elicited from the witness, it's a little circuitous to have the statement actually in front of the witness. I don't think the statement should actually be in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I do not see him reading. He needed it in order to identify the statement as his, the one he gave. Could you please try to keep in mind that leading to the extent not necessary should be avoided. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, I want to take you through the chronology of events when you arrived at Vuk Karadzic school, so if you could cast your mind back to standing at the entrance to the school, and then take me through which rooms you passed through and what you observed.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: As I entered the school, I was taken to a smallish room. They gave me a piece of paper and pencil and they ordered me to write what they wanted me to write. I refused to do that. They were angry. Then they said: Okay. We'll take you to the sports hall to witness how we are killing your people, and then you will start singing. They pushed me into the hall. They threw me on the ground. Then they made me watch how they were beating and killing people in the sports hall. Obviously, I was watching for a while, but then, with all that beating, I lost consciousness. When I came to, Branko Jovanovic approached me and told me that he would simply slaughter me, that he would cut my throat. He threatened me. He wanted me to confess things. I was confused. I said I didn't know anything about any of those things that he wanted me to write about. He took a knife and started beating me with the handle of the knife. At that moment, Krke appeared at the door, Novak, Stjepanovic, that is, the soldier that I had already described, and he said: Don't touch him. He approached me. He pushed Branko away and told me: They want to kill you, and I cannot allow that, because of the good relationship that we had in the mine. He took me out of the sports hall. I was bleeding from the wounds on my head. He took me to another room. He gave me a cigarette. I refused to take his cigarette. Then he gave me first aid. He dressed my wounds to stop the bleeding. He took me outside, inquired about my family, and then he told me: I can take you to the stadium to join your wife and your children, but I can't take you anywhere further. He did that. He brought me to the stadium gate and told me to enter the stadium. And he told me also: Serbs are going to live here. You have to go to Tuzla. In Tuzla, at the Tuzla stadium, 3.000 Serbs are incarcerated. We have to save them. I entered the stadium, and as I was walking across the stadium, I saw a couple of soldiers with loudspeakers. At least one of them had a megaphone. They were calling names, taking people from the stadium. I also saw people --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, can I stop you there. We will return to the events at the stadium. In the course of the answer to the last question, you mentioned that you were bleeding from wounds. How many wounds did you sustain?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I had two wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Where were those wounds?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: One was on the left side of my forehead, and the other one was on my right arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: How did you sustain those wounds?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I sustained those wounds from a soldier's army knife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Who was holding the knife when you sustained the wounds?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: It was Branko Jovanovic who hurt me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Who was Branko Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Branko Jovanovic was a citizen of Bratunac municipality, and at that moment, he wore a military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You also said earlier that you passed out. When you were in the sports hall, what happened to you, and why did you pass out?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I probably passed out due to the beating and the fear that I suffered at that moment. A fellow citizen of mine who was sitting next to me told me: You were unconscious. You were vomiting profusely, and I was really afraid that you might die.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In the sports hall, how many local Muslim men were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: In the sports hall, there were between 30 and 50 people who were being beaten constantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Were these people standing or lying, or in what position were they?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: On the left-hand side, some people were standing next to the wall, and they were constantly beaten with different objects. Some of the people had already been on the floor after the beatings that they had sustained. On the right-hand side, there were other people sitting on benches who were at that moment spared the beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: How many soldiers were in the sports hall with these 30 to 50 people?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Three soldiers were torturing and killing people, whereas the others were either guarding the door or they were standing in the corridors or they were in front of the entrance to the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Were these the same soldiers you've described earlier, that is, local soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: The ones at the entrance and in front of the entrance were soldiers from the town of Bratunac and the neighbouring republic, and in the school itself, there were soldiers who identified themselves as Arkan's men. They told us that they were paid to do what they were doing. And they also told us that they would make more money if they killed more people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: We will return to the description of those men. In the answer to the last question, you said, or the translation states that you referred to the town of Bratunac and the neighbouring republic. What do you mean by the "neighbouring republic"?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yugoslavia, which consisted of a number of republics. After the multi-party elections, there was another referendum on the independence of the states. The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina held a referendum, became an independent state, but we still continued referring to it as the neighbouring republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now I'll take you to the stadium, where you have told me Stjepanovic took you. How many people did you observe in the stadium when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: As I arrived at the stadium, there were a lot of people there; women, children, elderly. There were between four and five thousand people. Children were screaming. Women were crying. People in military uniforms were walking about, calling names. Any of them could call any name they wanted. They were looking for some individuals who were not even there. They collected all the possessions that the people had on them. They collected money, jewellery, they snatched earrings from children's ears. They threatened children that they would cut off their ears if they didn't give them their earrings, and then mothers would, in a haste, snatch those earrings from their children's ears and hand them over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: How many soldiers were present at the stadium, and did you recognise any of the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: At the stadium, because it is a very big stadium, I don't know exactly how many people there were, but the soldiers were going from one group of people to another, and I recognised many people by appearance, but I couldn't tell their names; at least, not for all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When you entered the stadium, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: After we spent quite a long time at that stadium, we were informed again through a megaphone that we were supposed to move. We started moving towards the gate, which had been opened. I happened to be close to the gate, and I moved along with my wife and children. We heard the buses and trucks that had been parked close to the stadium revving up and we were told that we were going to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When you reached the gate, what occurred?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: As I came to the gate, I saw a large number of soldiers on both sides of the gate. They separated young people, able-bodied men, on one side, and sent women and children to the buses. We, the able-bodied men, were directed to go in a double line towards the school building, the building of the Vuk Karadzic school. We were guarded by soldiers who flanked us. Krke told me that I was supposed to accompany my wife and children, so I protested, but they told me that there was no way I could go with my family, and they made me go to the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When you say "Krke told you that you were supposed to accompany your wife and children," are you referring to the conversation you had with Krke when he delivered you to the stadium?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I mean. A conversation we had before we came to the gate in front of the school building. We exchanged a few words and, among other things, he told me that he could not save me; all he could do is prevent them from killing me and try to make sure that I go to Tuzla. He asked me how many children I had. I was carrying one small child and had another child, the child of a cousin of mine, next to me. And he told me then: When you come up to the bus, tell them that I said you should go with your wife and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with Krke after you had met up with your family in the stadium?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The next day, around noon, Krke came to that school, saw me, and said: Oh, you are not gone. He came up to me and asked if I had been beaten. I said: Not recently. He said: Okay. Come here and sit on this bench. And then he summoned some men who were killing people. He told them: Bane Dragan, don't beat this man. He used to work in the mine with me. He's a good man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I will take you to that period of time when you were detained in the Vuk Karadzic school in a moment. Just taking you back to when the women and children and the men were separated at the stadium: Did you observe any other incidents at that time?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the stadium, I observed one incident when a man was pulled by the soldiers who were trying to force him to come along with them, and he was putting up a lot of resistance. I saw one of the soldiers get his knife at one point, stab the man, who fell on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What happened to your wife and children after the women and children were separated from the men?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: My wife and children, and the women who were residents of my neighbourhood in Suha, could not fit all into the buses that were provided, so they were told to go back home and spend the night there. They were told not to try to leave, but instead, to come the next morning to the same place, to board new buses that would take them to Tuzla. They said: If you comply, we guarantee the lives of your husbands. And of course, the women complied. My wife came the next morning to the stadium, where she was put, together with other women and children, on a bus, and they were taken to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I understand from your answers to the earlier questions that when you left the stadium, you were taken to the Vuk Karadzic school.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were taken again to the Vuk Karadzic school. This time we were a very large group of able-bodied men. However, there were some elderly men among us as well, aged over 60. They started cramming us into the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: How many men were taken to the school?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my rough estimate for that day would be 500 to 600 men taken to the school. However, every hour they would capture more people and bring them to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In the period of time that you were there, how many other men were captured and brought to the school?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: During the time that I spent there, during those three days, I believe a hundred more people were brought to the gym. Some were killed soon afterwards, some survived, but at any rate, new people kept coming all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When you arrived at the school after being brought from the stadium, what happened when this large group of men arrived at the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. entrance to the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, they couldn't fit all the people in, because the gym was too small, and then they threatened, and indeed later did so, that they would finish us off. A number of people were taken back outside, and we who stayed in that corridor, in that small hallway, were frightened to death when we heard shots outdoors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Approximately how many men were taken outside before you heard those shots?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I would say 10 or 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When this large group of men entered the sports hall, were they all standing in the hall or were they sitting, or in what posture were they?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: At first, during the first few hours, we were standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: After the first few hours, what occurred?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: After the first few hours, soldiers came into the gym, three soldiers. They took school benches, set them around the gym to create an open space in the middle, and then they started calling out names, asking if there was anyone who had worked in the SUP, anyone who had worked in schools, asking if there were any people present from Bratunac or from Potocari. And in the meantime, pieces of paper started going from hand to hand, passing to the guards, indicating names of people, and these people were later singled out, either for beatings and killing or just for beatings. After the beatings, some of the people crawled under the benches, and in several cases, such people survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Who provided the pieces of paper to the soldiers that were beating the people?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: These pieces of paper were passed by the guards who were standing near the door. They were wearing military uniforms. I just want to make you understand that anybody who wanted could go to the door. Some people came to the door of the gym in disguise; they didn't want us to recognise them. So they passed these pieces of paper with our names on it and we never really found out who they were, who provided this information to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: How were those people dressed?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the people who did the beating inside the gym?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No. The people that were passing the pieces of paper to the guards.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I said earlier that these pieces of paper were passed through the guards, and the people who wrote them were dressed -- I couldn't tell you how they were dressed. All I know is that the guards were in military uniform. But the person who did the beating would get the piece of paper directly from the guard or would simply bring the piece of paper himself, coming from the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: During the three days that you were in the sports hall, did you observe any people present around the sports hall in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In those three days that I spent in the gym, all of us Bosniaks who were detained were dressed in civilian clothes. However, at the door, and perhaps two metres inside the gym, Serb people dressed in civilian clothes would come and ask for some sort of information. Among them was a man from the SDS party, Miroslav Deronjic, who once came to the gym. I recognised him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Were any other people from the local authorities present at the door?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, because I didn't know everyone on the local authorities of Serb ethnicity. But from speaking to the people who did know them, I found out that almost all of them came at one point to visit. They would just come to the door, look in, and go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You said that the men who were detained were dressed in civilian clothes. Were they all civilians?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of those people were indeed civilians, and they were all rounded up in their own homes. A few of them were perhaps captured while trying to escape, or they were intercepted somewhere but mostly they were rounded up in their homes and in their basements. They simply went from house to house, looking for people to detain, and they didn't have a difficult job of it because people were hiding in groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What ethnicity were the people who were detained?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: The people detained in the Vuk Karadzic school were, for the most part, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Those who were not Muslims, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that there was anyone of a different ethnicity. Perhaps there were some gypsies, but even they called themselves Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You referred to three men who set up desks and an area in the sports hall. Can you describe those three men?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. One of the most prominent people introduced himself to us as Bane, also known as Zoka. He wore some sort of overalls. He was blond, tall, aged 30 or so. There was another man who gave us the name of Dragan. He was from Milici. He was strong, corpulent, wearing a military uniform. The third man, who did the torturing, called himself Zoka. He had a Macedonian accent, and therefore people called him "Macedonian." He was very much inclined to trouble-making. He was restless. He paced the room and he would go in and out of the gym all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did these men explain why they were there in the hall, doing what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They simply told us -- well, I can't say they told us they were sorry, but they said that they were given the job to kill people, that's what they were brought there for, and the more people they kill, the more money they will earn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt for one moment. You described three men. One of them, you said, that he introduced himself as Bane, also known as Zoka. And then when you described the third man, you said: The third man, who did the torturing, called himself Zoka. Do I understand well that there were two men who were called Zoka out of the three?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot tell you their real names with any degree of certainty. Those were the names they gave to us. The third man, as I told you, left the room all the time. He spoke with a Macedonian accent and he gave us his name as Zoka The Macedonian. But for the most part, everybody called him Macedonian. That's how the guards called him as well. He would come in and out of the gym, and he was dressed in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I do understand you well that two men out of the three were called Zoka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Over the next three days, what did these men do?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: In those three days, those three men beat up and killed people in the gym. They used all sorts of tools: Wooden handles of various tools, iron pipes, sometimes iron legs of a bed, I believe, and even the butts of pistols.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: How many men did you see them beat up or kill?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: What I can say with certainty is that they killed at least 50 people as I looked on; 50 that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Whilst they were beating the people, did they say anything?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They made all sorts of comments while they beat people. They issued threats. For instance, while they were beating one policeman, they told him: Oh, you are the one who shot at a Serb vehicle, puncturing the tyres. Then there was an old man who was the father of a shoemaker in Bratunac. I don't know his name. All I know is that he was very old and he had a bad back. When they were beating him, they said: Your son, Ismet, shot at our troops as they were going through the Hranca village towards Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did they make any comments about politics in the course of the three days?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were very political comments, such: You wanted a state. Here's your state for you. Or, for instance: Where is now your Alija to save you? On the third day, they brought a man from Potocari and they asked: Where is Naser, your liberator? On one occasion, I heard a sharp scream coming from a locker room where a man was being beaten, and they said: We just captured your liberator, Naser. Listen to him wailing in the locker room. He's now confessing as we speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did any senior military personnel enter the hall?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the second day. There was a very difficult moment for us. Those people who were beating us, holding those pipes and sticks, they were beating us, forced us to huddle in just one third of the room, and they kept beating us. And as they were beating us, we were forced to crawl on top of each other, almost up to the ceiling. At that point, a person in a military uniform, obviously of some high rank, came into the gym and said: What are you doing, men? Get off them. So he pulled them all outdoors. In fact, he told the guards to desist and we were able to occupy again the rest of the gym. As we got off each other, we noticed that perhaps seven or eight men had died under the stampede. Among the bodies was the body of a young man who was a locksmith in my mine, Husnija Hadzibulic. Another of the men who got killed by the stampede used to be a waiter, Omer; and I recognised another of the dead whose name was Hadzimuratovic. We dragged them all outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, may I ask you how much time you'd still need because we are close to the moment when we usually have a break but I've got no idea how much time we'd still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Probably most of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, this surprises me to the extent that it was indicated that, in order to have an opportunity to meet, that we would limit ourselves to one witness. But if the Defence needs some time for cross-examination as well, as I take it, then is it the absence of Mr. Harmon and Mr. Stewart that is at stake, or is it that we would shorten a bit our session of this morning? Because if you'd need another one hour and a half, then we might not even finish with this witness today, where I was asked not to start perhaps the next witness, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Mr. Harmon intends to lead the next witness that will be appearing after this witness, and we knew there was a possibility that this witness might take up the full day. But in the case that we finish sooner, we wanted to stop then and not require Mr. Harmon to come in and present the witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I now better understand. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with the comments from Mr. Hannis. That's basically the situation. I would just make one other comment in relation to my request for the summary earlier today. I'd indicate that perhaps it was not so much a sin of omission on Mr. Margetts' part; it's just that I'm used to Mr. Hannis giving me the summary every morning of the witness. So it's perhaps that I'm just being indulged by Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you how much time was scheduled for Mr. Hasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it was four and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. No. It's just not on the list, so I have to -- that's all understood. We'll then, if this would be a suitable moment, we'll adjourn until five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise for not having properly understood the suggestion made by the parties at the beginning of this session. It's now clear to me. Mr. Margetts, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Before that happens, actually, Your Honour, I think, depending on how long the rest of the examination-in-chief takes, and in view of the fact that we did want to have a further discussion today, it may be appropriate for me to commence my cross-examination tomorrow rather than after the end of the evidence in chief. I just want to forecast that, in terms of the time left available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we could look at that during the next break. Perhaps that's the most appropriate moment to consider where we stand.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also looking at the witness statement, I wonder whether you'd need the full session, Mr. Margetts. See what you can do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll do my best to expedite the remainder of the evidence. There is one matter, though, and that is that the witness statement did not fully explore the transport and events in Pale, and we provided some additional notes in respect of that to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, prior to the short break, you had identified various individuals who had suffocated in the Vuk Karadzic school. What happened to their bodies?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Their bodies were taken outside, and as far as I know, they were taken to a hangar that used to be used for practical work by children who went to that school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: After the commander left the building, did the three soldiers return?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe two hours later, these three soldiers returned to the sports hall and continued killing and beating people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: During the period that those three soldiers were absent from the hall and the commander was present, did you receive any food or water?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander ordered the guards to bring some food and water to the people, which was done. They brought us some sandwiches and some fruit juices. But this was sufficient for only half of the people there, so we struggled over that food and water.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Apart from that food and water, during the three days you were detained in the Vuk Karadzic school, did you receive any other sustenance?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't receive any food. On the following day, we got some more sandwiches, again too little, and then, on the third day, we were put on lorries and taken to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'm going to mention the names of various people, and if you could tell me whether or not you recognise those names and whether you know of anything that happened to those people. The first name is Zaim Huseinovic.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Zaim Huseinovic was an engineer who worked in the Srebrenica mine, where I worked as well. He was a very young man. He hid in Suha. He was captured together with the rest of us. He was brought to the sports hall. On one occasion they asked whether there was anybody from Potocari. Zaim stepped out. He is a native of Potocari, just like Naser Oric. The people who had beaten him before grabbed him, beat him again. He fell on the floor. Krke then appeared on the doorway and shouted to Bane: Bane, don't beat this man. He is an engineer that I know. He is a very quiet and peaceful man. He doesn't know anything about anything. And he snatched him away from Bane and set him beside me. When Krke left, either Bane or Dragan grabbed Zaim, hit him several times. They spilled his brains out. He died and then we were ordered to take his dead body out of the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'll take you to the events when you removed his body from the sports hall, but you mentioned that he was from Potocari. Was there any reason that they were targeting people from Srebrenica and Potocari?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is a good reason: Before our arrest, there was an incident in Potocari, during which a group of Arkan's men were killed in Potocari. And another reason is that before our arrest, Goran Zekic was killed. He was one of the deputies of the Srebrenica municipality. He was killed in an operation aimed at getting to Srebrenica, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: During the period that you were detained, did you see the father of Goran Zekic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Goran Zekic's father. He came to the sports hall one day. He came in civilian clothes. On the following day, he came in a military winter uniform. He asked us if we knew who had killed his son. He asked if there was anybody from Potocari. He said that he was sorry, but 300 people had to pay for the death of his son. And as far as I'm concerned, this is exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When you say they had to pay, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: They had to be killed, 300 people's lives had to be taken. They had to pay with their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: We were discussing the death of Zaim Huseinovic, and you said that the body was taken from the hangar. Can you please describe that. Apologies. A correction: You said it was taken from the sports hall. Can you describe please that.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: The ones who killed him decided that somebody was dead and that their body had to be taken out. They would then assign some detainees to take the body away. The four men would usually be assigned for that job. They would put the body onto a piece of cloth used for tents and then the body would be taken out of the sports hall by these four prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Were you assigned to take any bodies out?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, I was put in that situation. I was close to the door. I was sitting on a bench. One of the soldiers looked at me and said: Carry the body out. I approached the body. I don't know whose body it was, but I was the one who carried it to the hangar. As we entered the hangar, to our big surprise, we saw a man sitting amongst the bodies. He was delirious and he was covered with blood. We recognised him. He was strong and tall. He didn't have any hair on his head. His forehead was bloody. We told him to wipe his forehead, to put a clean T-shirt on, and we promised we would try to get him back to the sports hall. And this happened. The next group that were carrying the body, there were only three men in the group, and they took the body to the hangar, and then this man returned to the sports hall as the fourth carrier of the body. His name was Salko. He had been shot from a pistol. The bullet just scratched his forehead. He was probably unconscious when they took him to the hangar, believing that he was dead. However, he wasn't dead. He came to, and that's how he survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When you went to the hangar and saw Salko, how many other bodies did you see?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a roomful of bodies. I don't know how many exactly there were, but I would say that there were maybe 50 of them. It's very difficult to say. You have to understand that I was afraid. It was a long time ago. In any case, there was a heap of bodies. There was a large pile of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Do you know of a man named Zaimo [phoen] Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: His name was actually Dzemo Hodzic, not Zaimo Hodzic. I'd like to correct you on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Apologies. I am referring to Dzemo Hodzic. What happened to Dzemo Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Dzemo Hodzic was a reserve captain and he belonged to the defence of Bratunac. He worked in the military department during the peacetime. Dzemo Hodzic was afraid when the SDS came to power, and that's why he hid in the suburbs. He was captured in Suha. Suha was one of the safest places because of the population composition. Most of the people were Bosniaks. He was captured. He was brought to the sports hall. He had already been beaten. And they beat him there. He was dead. He was taken out. And a lorry was brought in to transport the bodies. Dzemo Hodzic was loaded onto the lorry. The window was open and we could hear his voice when he started shouting: Brethren, run away. You're going to be killed, all of you. Those of the men who had beaten him were -- got angry. They ordered the people to return him to the sports hall and they finished him off with wooden bats and metal rods. So finally he died, and he was taken out this time once for good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The next name I'll mention is that of the Muslim priest, Mustafa Mujkanovic. What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was the main Muslim priest in Bratunac, Mustafa Mujkanovic. He was a relative of mine. I knew him well. We even held some conversations before the occupation. We had close contacts. At one moment, when a guard at the door shouted: Oh, there is a hodza among them, then Bane said: Give us the hodza. They singled hodza out, they started beating him, without any previous explanations. He fell on the ground. They were drunk, and they had crates of beer. They forced him to drink beer, which he refused. Then they lifted him up, leaned him against the wall, forced him to lift three fingers. Mustafa didn't say a word. He just lifted two fingers. One of them noticed that. They were angry. They continued beating him. And Bane took out a knife. He hit him for the last time. Mustafa fell on the ground. As they were taking him out, he was still giving some signs of life; however, one of those murderers approached his body, took out a pistol, and shot a bullet in his head, and that's how they killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The next name I'll mention is that of Ramo Karic. What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Ramo Karic was my closest neighbour, whose house was five metres away from mine. His nickname was Krljo. He worked in the Vihor company. He was a lorry driver. A paper came through the door, asking for Ramo, the driver from Vihor. He stood up and said there were several of us called Ramo from Vihor. I'm Ramo called Krljo. And they said: Yes, we want you. They started beating him. Bane took out a pistol from his pocket. He shot a bullet into his elbow. Ramo screamed, bent over. They continued beating him and they killed him there on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Was your cousin Ahmet Salkic detained? What happened?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Ahmet Salkic was detained, and I believe that I personally took his body out. He was killed very soon. He was physically weak and it took just one blow to kill him. He had blond hair, long hair, and a green jacket. And they said: There is an Ustasha. And one of them hit him in the forehead, close to the eye. He fell on the ground and he sustained another blow, which was probably lethal, and then we were ordered to carry his body out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Next name, Hajrudin Comic. What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Hajrudin Comic. I knew him. He was prone to drinking. They gave him a beer to drink, and he drank it so fast that Bane said: Look at him drinking. He ordered him to kneel and he fired a shot either into his head or into his neck, and he died of that wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Next name is that of Mensur Husic. What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Mensur Husic is also from Suha, another neighbour of mine. He was blond and that's why we called him Zuco. He was brought to the sports hall the third day, just before our departure for Pale. They brought him and they found a place amongst us who were his neighbour. He told us that he had been captured on the way to the police station. He was brought to the sports hall. He told us that we were supposed to go to Pale. At one point he stood up and said he wanted to find his suitcase, where supposedly there were clothes for his wife and for his baby, who had already been transported to Tuzla. When he returned, he was frightened and very pale, and he started stuttering. At the same moment, his name was called out. They said: Zuco, the tractor driver, come out. He stood up. I believe that he knew what was to be his lot. He started screaming. And they started beating him already at the doorstep. At one point, I heard him screaming: Don't kill me. He was taken out. I heard a burst of fire, and another scream of his, which was rather loud, but after that, I did not hear him screaming any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did you know a policeman whose first name was Mustafa? If so, what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew the policeman Mustafa. He was a single young man from Suha. They took him out, they beat him, they told him that he was the man who shot at a Serb lorry when the Serb lorry wouldn't stop. They beat him. He was lucky to survive, because while Bane and the others who were -- had been beating him were taking a rest, we pulled him amongst ourselves. We hid him among a bench. He was beaten all over, but he managed to survive and he was finally exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In total, how many men did you see beaten to death or shot to death?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I personally witnessed at least 50 people being killed by different objects and in various manners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Apart from those beatings and killings you witnessed, were other men called out from the hall?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Other people's names were called out. The majority of people responded to those call-outs. On one occasion they called my name out, and my relative then said he was taken away from the school yard yesterday, and from then on, I decided not to respond to the call-outs, and that's how I managed to remain among the people in the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Of the men who initially were taken from the stadium to the sports hall, and the men that arrived at the sports hall during your detention there, how many do you estimate were killed in that three-day period?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'd object to the form of that question as to whether the Prosecutor is asking about actual killings witnessed or killings he might have heard about. I think it should be specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, first of all, the witness had already testified that he personally saw 50 people being killed over the next three days, as far as I understand. You find that in page 30, line 10 and following. So that is a repetitious question. He also testified that at a certain moment he approximately saw in the room some 50 bodies of people killed. He explained how bodies were loaded on trucks. So whether a further estimate where he said that I think four to five hundred people were in the school and frequently taken out, I don't know whether that really assists the Chamber in order to have more guesses in that respect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When new arrivals came to the sports hall, what did they tell the detainees in the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: All the new arrivals told us that there was a hell outside, that there were bodies lying all around, that people are being captured, that neighbouring villages were ablaze, that the situation was really difficult. And that pretty much sums it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Were you taken from the Vuk Karadzic school at some point; and if so, can you describe that?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: On the first day when I was brought in, Krke took me to the stadium, but on that same day I returned with a big group of people back to the school. I was not taken out of the school. Some people were taken from the school in some way. Some of them returned. I don't know what happened to them and what was their lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: After the period of three days when you were detained in the Vuk Karadzic school, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: After three days, late in the evening, we heard lorries with soft canvas cover. They stopped in front of the sports hall and we were told that we would be exchanged. We rushed to the lorries. We couldn't wait to be exchanged. We were all loaded onto the lorries, and when almost half of us were already on the lorries, somebody came and asked for some people. Some of them were already on the lorries so some people had to get off. Some 10 or 20 people remained in the sports hall, and they did not join us on our way to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You said some people had to get off. Why did they have to get off?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know why. Their names were called. I don't know who called their names. A list appeared and we were told that the people on the list were not to be allowed to go to Pale to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: How many lorries were there?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: There were four lorries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Approximately how many men were on each lorry?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately a hundred men were on each lorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the drivers of the lorries?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised one driver, who worked in the Vihor company. And he also used to work with a relative of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: His name was Rocko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: At what time were you loaded onto these lorries?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: We were loaded onto the lorries in the very late hours of the evening or the early hours of the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to show the witness the exhibit that was previously marked as Prosecution Exhibit P61. May this exhibit be presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, could you please turn to the page which is numbered 13 in the top right-hand corner and marked for identification 0083-5787.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, if you could guide those who are reading English to the relevant page as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you could turn to page 11 of the English translation, which is marked at the top with the last four digits 1271.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, does your name appear on that page?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It appears on page number 13, Resid Hasanovic, born in Bratunac, residing in Suha.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And could you read out what is written beside your name.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: My father's name, the year when I was born, where I was born, and the village where I resided, or the neighbourhood, the name of the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And your father's name was Hasan, you were born in 1958, and you resided in Suha; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Could you look through that document and could you tell me whether you recognise other names listed in this document.

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know a lot of people from this document. They are mainly people from the areas of Suha, Mihaljevici, and Ravne. There were also a number of people who were simply hiding in that area. The others I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Does this appear to you to contain the names of many of the men who were detained in the Vuk Karadzic school and transported on the evening of 13 May 1992?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that this list contains the largest majority of even 100 per cent of the people who were transported to Pale and later exchanged in Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: During the course of the journey from the Vuk Karadzic school, did the trucks stop at any point?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They stopped in the morning, around dawn. I think that intersection was called Semizovac. They pulled up the tarpaulins covering the lorries. Some people who were huddled inside recognised the road. They had recognised it even earlier, looking through the little holes in the tarpaulin. We noticed around the lorries policemen dressed in uniforms of Republika Srpska. They were rather kind and gave us water to drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Apart from the lorries, did you observe any other vehicles travelling with the lorries?

utterances.speaker: RESID HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just before we set out, we were warned that it is not a good idea to try to run, that we were being taken to be exchanged, that rescue is near, and we believed them.
